elements.quote: This version is update 1 of the original article published on 16 March 2022 ( BMJ 2022;376:e067696), and previous updates can be found as data supplements
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies itself as an update of a previous version and cites the original article (BMJ 2022;376:e067696), but the retrieved evidence does not show an explicit explanation in the introduction of why the update was needed.
This is a review of SARS-CoV-2 transmission rates, not a review of intervention effects, so no mechanism of action applies.
This is a review of infection transmission, not of complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: To assess the rates of SARS-CoV-2 positivity in babies born to mothers with SARS-CoV-2 infection, the timing of mother-to-child transmission and perinatal outcomes, and factors associated with SARS-CoV-2 status in offspring.
elements.reason: The objectives are explicitly stated in the 'Abstract > Objectives' section, covering all review aims (rates of positivity, timing of transmission, perinatal outcomes, associated factors).
This is a review of prevalence/rates and transmission timing, not a review of intervention effects, so planned comparisons in PICO format are not required.

elements.quote: we included cohort studies of pregnant and recently pregnant women who sought hospital care for any reason and had a diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection, and where SARSCoV-2 status was ascertained in the fetus or neonate using RT-PCR ... or serological tests (antiSARS-CoV-2 IgM), or both. We defined cohort studies as those that sampled consecutive women, who were followed-up to ascertain the SARS-CoV-2 status of their offspring within the first 30 days after birth.
elements.reason: Study designs (cohorts, case series/reports), population, exposure, outcome ascertainment tests, and follow-up requirements (within first 30 days) are clearly specified for each synthesis aim.

elements.quote: For this update of the living systematic review, we included studies from searches up to 25 April 2022. No language restrictions were applied.
elements.reason: Language (no restrictions) and a search date limit are reported, but publication status restrictions are not explicitly stated as eligibility criteria.
No evidence distinguishes exclusion of studies because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: To assess SARSCoV-2 positivity rates in offspring, we included cohort studies... In addition to the cohort studies, we included case series and case reports to assess the timing of motherto-child transmission and likelihood of infection. To evaluate maternal risk factors for offspring SARS-CoV-2 positivity, we included cohort studies... that reported on maternal and perinatal risk factors such as maternal severe covid-19... mode of delivery (caesarean section v vaginal birth)...
elements.reason: Groups for each synthesis (positivity rates, timing of transmission, risk factor comparisons) are specified and linked to the review objectives and comparisons.

elements.quote: We only included cohort studies for estimating the rates of SARS-CoV-2 positivity in offspring, unlike some of the published systematic reviews, which combined cohort and case-control studies with case series
elements.reason: A rationale for the notable restriction to cohort studies for estimating positivity rates is provided in the strengths section.

elements.reason: Search date (25 April 2022) is reported; text_5 also states coverage 'between 1 December 2019 and 25 April 2022'.

elements.reason: Database names are given, but search interfaces/platforms and coverage dates per database are not specified.

elements.reason: Preprint servers and repositories mentioned generically; specific register names and date restrictions not fully reported.

elements.reason: Websites mentioned but no names or URLs provided.

elements.quote: We searched major databases, preprint servers, and websites that serve as repositories for covid-19 studies, including Medline, Embase, Cochrane database, WHO COVID-19 database, Living Overview of the Evidence platform, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang databases ... Our searches were coordinated with the EPPI-Centre, the WHO (World Health Organization) Library, and the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility group (see supplementary appendix 2).
elements.reason: All databases, registers, and websites searched are named, and the full search strategies appear to be provided in supplementary appendix 2, but the complete search strings are not reported in the retrieved main-text evidence.

elements.quote: For this update of the living systematic review, we included studies from searches up to 25 April 2022. No language restrictions were applied.
elements.reason: Date limits (1 December 2019 to 25 April 2022, per text_5) and absence of language restrictions are reported, but these limits are not explicitly justified by reference to the eligibility criteria.
No published search approaches, filters, or adaptations are cited in the retrieved evidence.
No evidence that natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were used to identify or refine search terms.
No evidence that tools were used to translate search strings between sources.
No validation of the search strategy is described in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is described in the retrieved evidence.
No evidence indicates the search structure was not based on PICO; the conceptual structure is not discussed in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Eighteen reviewers contributed to study selection. Two independent reviewers assessed each study using a two stage process. In the first stage, the titles and abstracts of all citations were screened, and the full texts examined for inclusion in the second stage.
elements.reason: Number of reviewers (two per study) is specified for both screening stages (titles/abstracts and full texts).

elements.quote: Two independent reviewers assessed each study using a two stage process.
elements.reason: Independence of reviewers is explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer (ST, JA, or SF-G).
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution process is described.
No description of contacting investigators to obtain or confirm eligibility information for screening; only data duplication queries are mentioned (text_16), which is not eligibility confirmation.
No mention of translation of non-English abstracts or articles for eligibility assessment.
No automation tools described in the selection process.
No externally derived classifiers used, so requirement does not apply.
No internally derived classifiers used.
No machine-learning prioritisation or stopping rules reported.
No crowdsourcing platforms used.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records before screening.

elements.quote: Using a pre-piloted form, six independent reviewers in two sets extracted data on study design, number of pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 infection...
elements.reason: The number of reviewers collecting data is explicitly reported (six independent reviewers in two sets; also 'Two reviewers independently extracted data' in text_7).

elements.quote: Using a pre-piloted form, six independent reviewers in two sets extracted data
elements.reason: Independent working of data extractors is explicitly stated.
No evidence describes processes for resolving disagreements between data collectors.

elements.quote: We contacted study authors for unpublished information and to query duplication of data.
elements.reason: The process for obtaining or confirming data from study investigators is described.
No automation tools used in data collection are reported in the retrieved evidence.

No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported; only 'No language restrictions were applied' in searching (text_14), which does not describe translation of articles for extraction.
No software used to extract data from figures is specified in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: A detailed deduplication process was used to cross check data against other studies published by the same authors or those that included women from the same institutions.
elements.reason: A process for handling overlapping/multiple reports (deduplication cross-check) is described, but specific decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports and resolving inconsistencies are not fully detailed.

elements.quote: extracted data on study design, number of pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 infection, type of SARS-CoV-2 test in mothers and babies (RT-PCR, IgM), maternal characteristics (including stage of pregnancy at diagnosis), severity of covid-19 (as defined by authors), mode of delivery, type of samples tested..., timing of sample collection, and SARS-CoV-2 predominant variant of concern... We also extracted data on the clinical outcomes of all SARSCoV-2 positive fetuses and neonates when available, including early pregnancy outcomes of miscarriage and abortion.
elements.reason: The data items sought are listed (offspring SARS-CoV-2 positivity, timing of transmission via WHO classification, clinical outcomes), but outcome domains are not formally listed and defined as a distinct set; definitions rely on author definitions or WHO classification.

elements.quote: timing of sample collection
elements.reason: Timing of sample collection was extracted and transmission timing was categorised (in utero, intrapartum, early postnatal per text_7), but an explicit time frame of measurement for each outcome domain is not systematically specified.
No statement indicates whether all compatible results within each outcome domain (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.
No process for selecting among compatible results is described in the retrieved evidence.
No changes to outcome definitions or their importance with rationales are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No changes to processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported.
The retrieved evidence does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions or a rationale for prioritisation.

elements.quote: Using a pre-piloted form, six independent reviewers in two sets extracted data on study design, number of pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 infection, type of SARS-CoV-2 test in mothers and babies (RT-PCR, IgM), maternal characteristics (including stage of pregnancy at diagnosis), severity of covid-19 (as defined by authors), mode of delivery, type of samples tested (neonatal nasopharyngeal, rectal, or faecal swabs, neonatal or cord blood, fetal tissue, placenta, amniotic fluid, vaginal fluid, breast milk), timing of sample collection, and SARS-CoV-2 predominant variant of concern
elements.reason: The data extraction section comprehensively lists the variables sought, including definitions such as severity of covid-19 'as defined by authors' and variant mapping approach.

elements.quote: SARS-CoV-2 predominant variant of concern 20 (as reported by authors, or mapped to the dominant variant in the country during the study period using https://covariants.org/)
elements.reason: Assumptions about unclear information are described: variants not reported by authors were mapped to the dominant country variant, and WHO classification with added categories was used to classify timing of transmission when tests were incomplete (per Fig 3 footnotes).

No evidence of a tool used to determine which data items to collect; data items were determined by the authors' pre-piloted form and registered protocol, so this conditional requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: We assessed the internal and external validity of non-comparative cohorts using the tool by Hoy et al. 18 ... We assessed the methodological quality of the comparative cohort studies using the Newcastle Ottawa scale
elements.reason: Two risk-of-bias tools are explicitly named: the Hoy et al. tool for non-comparative cohorts and the Newcastle Ottawa Scale for comparative cohorts.

elements.quote: For internal validity, we considered studies to be at low risk of bias if data were collected from clinical records or research case report forms (data collection), clearly defined outcomes (case definition), confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection using laboratory based tests (instrument validity)... We assessed the methodological quality of the comparative cohort studies using the Newcastle Ottawa scale for selection, comparability, and outcome ascertainment bias outcome.
elements.reason: The domains/items of both tools are specified: data collection, case definition, instrument validity, ascertainment bias, follow-up for Hoy et al.; selection, comparability, and outcome for NOS.

elements.quote: The overall risk of bias (Newcastle Ottawa scale) for the included comparative cohort studies was low in 98% (89/91) of studies
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement is reported for the NOS-assessed studies, but the rules used to derive the overall judgement are not explicitly described for either tool.
No evidence of adaptations to an existing risk-of-bias tool; standard tools (Hoy et al., NOS) were used as described.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is reported; existing published tools were used.

elements.quote: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality.
elements.reason: Number of reviewers (two) and independence are reported for quality assessment, but disagreement-resolution procedures specific to risk-of-bias assessment are not described (disagreement resolution is mentioned only for study selection in text_15).
No process for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators is reported; author contact related to data duplication/unpublished data, not risk of bias.
No automation tools are reported as being used for risk-of-bias assessment.

elements.quote: A random effects model was used to synthesise data for rates, with associations reported using odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Narrative syntheses were performed when meta-analysis was inappropriate.
elements.reason: The methods specify the effect measure for each outcome type: rates/proportions for SARS-CoV-2 positivity in offspring (further detailed in text_17: 'After transforming data using Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation, we used DerSimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis to calculate rates and corresponding 95% confidence intervals'), odds ratios with 95% CIs for associations between maternal/perinatal factors and offspring positivity (text_17: 'we pooled comparative dichotomous data as odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals using random effects meta-analysis'), and narrative descriptive synthesis for outcomes where meta-analysis was inappropriate (e.g., clinical outcomes in test-positive babies).

No thresholds or ranges for interpreting the magnitude of effect sizes (e.g., minimal important differences) are mentioned anywhere in the retrieved evidence; the review presents effect estimates with 95% CIs without applying interpretive thresholds, so this conditional requirement does not apply.

The retrieved evidence describes no re-expression of synthesized results into a different effect measure (e.g., converting odds ratios to risk ratios). The Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation is a variance-stabilizing transformation used to pool proportions, not a re-expression of results using another effect measure, so this conditional requirement does not apply.

Although odds ratios (for comparative dichotomous data) and proportions/rates (for positivity) are specified as effect measures, no rationale or justification for choosing these effect measures is provided anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: To assess SARSCoV-2 positivity rates in offspring, we included cohort studies of pregnant and recently pregnant women who sought hospital care for any reason and had a diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection... In addition to the cohort studies, we included case series and case reports to assess the timing of motherto-child transmission and likelihood of infection. To evaluate maternal risk factors for offspring SARS-CoV-2 positivity, we included cohort studies of pregnant and recently pregnant women with a diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection that reported on maternal and perinatal risk factors such as maternal severe covid-19, admission to an intensive care unit, and death...
elements.reason: The Study Selection section explicitly specifies which study designs and characteristics were eligible for each planned synthesis (positivity rates, timing of transmission, and maternal risk factors), describing the processes used to decide eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote: After transforming data using Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation, we used DerSimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis to calculate rates and corresponding 95% confidence intervals.
elements.reason: The Data Analysis section describes data preparation methods including the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation for proportions, pooling dichotomous data as odds ratios, classification of babies into mutually exclusive transmission categories (with modifications to WHO criteria), and a detailed deduplication process with author contact for missing/unpublished information (text_16: 'A detailed deduplication process was used... We contacted study authors for unpublished information').

No methods text describes the tabular structures used to display results or the data included in them; tables (e.g., Table 4) are present in results but their construction is not described in the methods.

elements.quote: A random effects model was used to synthesise data for rates, with associations reported using odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals.
elements.reason: The methods describe the statistical synthesis (random effects model) but do not describe any graphical display methods such as forest plots or funnel plots, even though figures exist.
No statement on the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs is provided in the retrieved evidence.
No rationale for using non-standard graphs is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: All statistical analyses were performed using Stata (version 16).
elements.reason: Software and version number for statistical synthesis are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: When metaanalysis was considered inappropriate because of excessive clinical or statistical heterogeneity or when SARS-CoV-2 positive offspring were selectively reported in the cohort studies, we used a narrative descriptive approach to summarise the evidence
elements.reason: Alternative narrative synthesis is described and the rationale for its use is provided.

elements.quote: we used DerSimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis to calculate rates and corresponding 95% confidence intervals
elements.reason: The random-effects model is named for each meta-analysis, but no explicit rationale for choosing the model is given.

elements.quote: After transforming data using Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation, we used DerSimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis to calculate rates
elements.reason: Statistical method (Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation with DerSimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis) is reported for the rate meta-analysis, and random effects pooling of odds ratios is also described.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was reported as I 2 and τ 2 estimates.
elements.reason: Methods to identify and quantify statistical heterogeneity (I² and τ²) are reported.

elements.quote: we used DerSimonian and Laird random effects meta-analysis
elements.reason: The between-study variance estimator (DerSimonian and Laird) is explicitly named.
95% confidence intervals are reported but the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect (e.g., Wald-type, Knapp-Hartung) is not stated.
No additional random-effects implementation details beyond the model and estimator are reported.
Bayesian meta-analysis was not used; only frequentist (DerSimonian and Laird) random effects methods are described.

Statistical methods to account for dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., multiple variants, multiple samples) are not described; only a data deduplication process is mentioned, which is not a statistical synthesis method for dependency.

elements.quote: When metaanalysis was considered inappropriate because of excessive clinical or statistical heterogeneity or when SARS-CoV-2 positive offspring were selectively reported in the cohort studies, we used a narrative descriptive approach
elements.reason: Situations where planned meta-analysis was inappropriate are identified with explicit reasons, and narrative synthesis was used instead.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analysis for SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates in babies was done by restricting the analysis to studies at low risk of bias, babies tested at less than 24 h after birth, and babies born to mothers with SARS-CoV-2 infection diagnosed antenatally. The rates of SARSCoV-2 positivity were also evaluated by subgroups of studies involving babies and mothers from various World Bank regions and by predominant SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern.
elements.reason: Methods to explore heterogeneity (sensitivity and subgroup analyses) are explicitly described.

elements.quote: The rates of SARSCoV-2 positivity were also evaluated by subgroups of studies involving babies and mothers from various World Bank regions and by predominant SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern.
elements.reason: Subgroup factors and levels (World Bank regions, variants of concern, risk of bias, timing of testing/infection) are reported, but no expected direction of effect modification is stated.
No statement clarifies whether subgroup analyses used study-level variables or within-study contrasts.
No method for comparing subgroup effects (e.g., interaction tests or difference tests) is reported; only subgroup estimates are described.

elements.quote: When metaanalysis was considered inappropriate because of excessive clinical or statistical heterogeneity or when SARS-CoV-2 positive offspring were selectively reported in the cohort studies, we used a narrative descriptive approach to summarise the evidence, such as for clinical outcomes in test positive babies and test positivity in various biological samples.
elements.reason: Informal narrative synthesis when meta-analysis was unsuitable is described with examples, but specific factors and levels for informal heterogeneity exploration are not detailed.
The manuscript does not identify which heterogeneity analyses were not pre-specified, although a prospective protocol is referenced.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analysis for SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates in babies was done by restricting the analysis to studies at low risk of bias, babies tested at less than 24 h after birth, and babies born to mothers with SARS-CoV-2 infection diagnosed antenatally.
elements.reason: The Data Analysis section describes the sensitivity analyses performed (restriction to low risk of bias studies, testing <24 h, antenatal diagnosis), and results of these analyses are reported in text_22.

The manuscript does not indicate whether the sensitivity analyses were pre-specified or identify any as post hoc; no such statement appears in the retrieved evidence, and the protocol registration mention does not cover sensitivity analyses.

No methods for assessing risk of bias due to missing results (reporting biases) are described anywhere in the retrieved evidence. The manuscript only describes study quality assessment tools (Hoy et al. tool, Newcastle Ottawa scale) for internal/external validity of included studies, not methods for assessing reporting biases or missing results in the synthesis.

No reporting-bias assessment tool (e.g., funnel plot asymmetry tests) was used for assessing missing results, so there are no domains or overall judgement processes of such a tool to report. The Newcastle Ottawa scale and Hoy et al. tool relate to risk of bias in individual studies, a different PRISMA item.
No existing reporting-bias tool was adapted, as no reporting-bias assessment was performed according to the retrieved evidence.
No newly developed reporting-bias tool is described or referenced in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (two; also 'six independent reviewers in two sets' in text_16) and their independence are reported for study quality assessment. However, no disagreement-resolution procedure is reported specifically for quality/risk-of-bias assessment; a third-reviewer resolution process is mentioned only for study selection (text_15).

This element is conditional on a reporting-bias assessment being performed. No reporting-bias assessment is described, although author contact is reported for missing transmission-classification data (text_16), which pertains to data completeness, not reporting-bias assessment.
No automation tools are reported as being used for reporting-bias assessment (or any assessment) in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We assessed the internal and external validity of non-comparative cohorts using the tool by Hoy et al. ... We assessed the methodological quality of the comparative cohort studies using the Newcastle Ottawa scale
elements.reason: The manuscript describes risk-of-bias/methodological quality tools (Hoy et al., Newcastle Ottawa scale) for individual studies, but no tool for assessing certainty/confidence in the body of evidence (e.g., GRADE) is reported.

No factors or criteria for assessing certainty in the body of evidence are reported; only study-level risk-of-bias criteria (Hoy tool, NOS) are described, which does not constitute certainty-of-evidence assessment.
No decision rules or interpretation of certainty levels for outcomes are described anywhere in the retrieved evidence.
No body-of-evidence certainty assessment (e.g., GRADE) is reported, so review-specific certainty thresholds and rationales do not apply.
Since no certainty-assessment system is used or reported, adaptations to such a system do not apply.

elements.quote: Using a pre-piloted form, six independent reviewers in two sets extracted data
elements.reason: Reviewer numbers and independence are reported only for data extraction and study selection, not for a certainty-of-evidence assessment, which is not described.
No certainty assessment of the body of evidence was performed, so processes for obtaining/confirming information from investigators for that purpose do not apply.
